children.title: Administrative Info
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Administrative Info
children.summary: This page provides administrative details for a course, including class times (Fridays 14:00-15:30), location (Ground Floor Lecture Theater, Wilkins Building), and office hours. It lists the Teaching Assistant as Giulia Luise and provides contact information via website, email, and physical address at UCL. The workload section outlines that the grade is split between two assignments (50%) and a final exam (50%), with specific requirements for the exam questions.

children.title: Course Material
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Course Material
children.summary: This page lists the main resources for a course, including classes and slides. It also details several books and other materials relevant to Statistical Learning Theory, such as 'Understanding Machine Learning' by Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, and course notes from Stanford.

children.title: Prerequisites
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Prerequisites
children.summary: The page lists the academic prerequisites required for a course or topic. It outlines three main areas of study: Linear Algebra, Calculus, and Probability Theory, providing specific examples of concepts within each field such as matrix operations, limits, and probability distributions.

children.title: Statistical Learning Theory (SLT)
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Statistical Learning Theory (SLT)
children.summary: This page introduces Statistical Learning Theory (SLT), outlining its primary objectives such as defining what it means for an algorithm to learn and how to design efficient algorithms. It further explains that SLT studies theoretical quantities not directly accessible, aiming to bridge the gap between unknown functional relations and finite empirical observations.

children.title: Motivations and Examples: Regression
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Motivations and Examples: Regression
children.summary: The page is titled 'Motivations and Examples: Regression' and illustrates the concept of regression analysis using housing data. On the left, a table lists specific examples of living area in square feet alongside corresponding house prices in thousands of dollars. On the right, a scatter plot visualizes this relationship, plotting price against square footage to show a positive correlation.

children.title: Motivations and Examples: Binary Classification
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Motivations and Examples: Binary Classification

children.title: Spam detection
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Motivations and Examples: Binary Classification/Spam detection
children.summary: The section titled 'Spam detection' describes the task of automatically discriminating between spam and non-spam emails. It illustrates this as a binary classification problem where an input (represented by documents) is mapped to one of two output classes: 'legit' or 'spam'.

children.title: Image Classification
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Motivations and Examples: Binary Classification/Image Classification
children.summary: The section titled 'Image Classification' illustrates a binary classification task where an input image of a dog is processed by a function f to determine if it belongs to the class 'dog' or 'not dog'.

children.title: Motivations and Examples: Multi-class Classification
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Motivations and Examples: Multi-class Classification
children.summary: The section titled 'Motivations and Examples: Multi-class Classification' introduces the task of identifying object categories in images. It begins with a simple example using the Caltech 101 dataset, showing sample images for classes like baseball-bat, dog, basketball-hoop, kayak, and traffic light. The content then scales up to discuss the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, which involves detecting correct objects among thousands of categories.

children.title: Motivations and Examples: Structured Prediction
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Motivations and Examples: Structured Prediction
children.summary: The page is a presentation slide titled 'Motivations and Examples: Structured Prediction'. It illustrates four distinct applications of structured prediction through visual examples: Image Captioning (showing object localization and classification), Movie Ranking (using Netflix as an example to show user preference ordering), Speech Recognition (depicting the phrase 'Ok Google'), and Protein Folding (showing the transition from a sequence to a 3D structure).

children.title: Formulating The Learning Problem
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem
children.summary: This section outlines the main ingredients for formulating a learning problem: input and output spaces (X and Y), an unknown distribution (ρ) on their product space, and a loss function (ℓ). It defines the objective as minimizing the expected risk E(f), which represents the expected prediction error incurred by a predictor f.

children.title: Input Space
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Input Space

children.title: Linear Spaces
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Input Space/Linear Spaces
children.summary: The section titled 'Linear Spaces' lists three types of mathematical objects that fall under this category: Vectors, Matrices, and Functions.

children.title: "Structured" Spaces
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Input Space/"Structured" Spaces
children.summary: The section titled "Structured" Spaces" lists examples of non-linear data structures used as input spaces, including strings, graphs, probabilities, and points on a manifold.

children.title: Output Space
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Output Space

children.title: Linear Spaces, e.g.
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Output Space/Linear Spaces, e.g.
children.summary: The section titled 'Linear Spaces, e.g.' lists three examples of linear output spaces used in machine learning: regression (where the output space is the set of real numbers), classification (where the output space is a finite set of integers from 1 to T), and multi-task learning (where the output space is a vector space of dimension T).

children.title: "Structured" Spaces, e.g.
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Output Space/"Structured" Spaces, e.g.
children.summary: The section titled "Structured" Spaces, e.g. lists examples of structured output spaces used in machine learning or related fields. These include Strings, Graphs, Probabilities, and Orders (specifically Ranking), indicating types of outputs that have internal structure beyond simple linear values.

children.title: Probability Distribution
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Probability Distribution
children.summary: The page defines the concept of a probability distribution, denoted as ρ on X × Y. It explains that this distribution encodes the probability of observing a pair (x, y) from an unknown process. The text further breaks down the joint distribution into its components: the marginal distribution on X and the conditional distribution on Y given x.

children.title: Conditional Distribution
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Conditional Distribution
children.summary: The page defines the concept of a conditional distribution, denoted as ρ(y|x), which characterizes the relationship between an input x and possible outcomes y. It explains that in noisy settings, this represents uncertainty. An example is provided where y equals a true function f*(x) plus Gaussian distributed noise ε, leading to the conclusion that the conditional distribution is a normal distribution centered at f*(x).

children.title: Loss Functions
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Loss Functions
children.summary: This page defines the concept of a loss function in machine learning, denoted as ℓ. It explains that the loss function represents the cost incurred when predicting f(x) instead of the true value y. The text further presents the mathematical formulation for expected risk, E(f), defined as the integral of the loss over the probability distribution ρ(x,y).

children.title: Loss Functions for Regression
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Loss Functions/Loss Functions for Regression
children.summary: The page presents a slide titled 'Loss Functions for Regression,' which defines three common loss functions used in machine learning: Square loss, Absolute loss, and epsilon-insensitive loss. It provides the mathematical formula for each function and includes a chart that visually compares their behavior over a range of values from -1.0 to 1.0.

children.title: Loss Functions for Classification
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Formulating The Learning Problem/Loss Functions/Loss Functions for Classification
children.summary: The section titled 'Loss Functions for Classification' defines the general property of a loss function L(y, y') = L(-yy'). It then lists four specific types of loss functions used in classification: 0-1 loss, Square loss, Hinge-loss, and logistic loss, providing the mathematical formula for each. A graph at the bottom visualizes these four loss functions over a range of values.

children.title: Defining Learning Algorithms
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Defining Learning Algorithms
children.summary: The section defines learning algorithms as maps from datasets to functions, introduces non-deterministic (stochastic) algorithms where the output is a distribution rather than a fixed function, and formulates the learning problem by defining 'good' predictors in terms of minimizing excess risk relative to the best possible solution.

children.title: The Elements of Learning Theory
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory
children.summary: The Elements of Learning Theory

children.title: Consistency
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency
children.summary: This page defines the concept of consistency in learning algorithms. It states that an algorithm is consistent if, as the sample size approaches infinity, the error of the learned function converges to the infimum of the error over all possible functions. The text notes that since the training set is randomly sampled, the learned function is a random variable, and poses the question of how to interpret this convergence.

children.title: Convergence of Random Variables
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency/Convergence of Random Variables

children.title: Convergence in expectation:
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency/Convergence of Random Variables/Convergence in expectation:
children.summary: The section defines convergence in expectation, stating that the limit as n approaches infinity of the expected value of the difference between E(f_n) and the infimum of E(f) over f in F is equal to zero.

children.title: Convergence in probability:
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency/Convergence of Random Variables/Convergence in probability:
children.summary: The section titled 'Convergence in probability' defines this concept using a mathematical limit formula. It states that the probability of the difference between E(f_n) and the infimum of E(f) over F being greater than epsilon approaches zero as n approaches infinity, for all epsilon greater than 0.

children.title: Consistency vs Convergence of the Estimator
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency/Consistency vs Convergence of the Estimator
children.summary: The page discusses the distinction between consistency and convergence of an estimator, focusing on the goal of ensuring that the risk of an estimator converges to the best possible value. It presents mathematical expressions defining this convergence and contrasts it with determining whether a sequence of estimators converges to a minimizer of the expected risk. The text notes that in some cases, such as compressive sensing and inverse problems, a minimizer may not exist.

children.title: Existence of a Minimizer for the Risk
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency/Existence of a Minimizer for the Risk

children.title: Least Squares.
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency/Existence of a Minimizer for the Risk/Least Squares.
children.summary: The section defines the Least Squares loss function as ℓ(f(x), y) = (f(x) - y)^2. It presents a mathematical relationship showing that the difference in risk between a function f and its minimizer f* is equal to the squared L2 norm of their difference, specifically ||f - f*||_{L^2(X, ρ)}.

children.title: Lipschitz Loss.
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Consistency/Existence of a Minimizer for the Risk/Lipschitz Loss.
children.summary: The section titled 'Lipschitz Loss' defines the Lipschitz condition for a loss function, stating that the difference in loss values is bounded by a constant L times the distance between inputs. It presents the resulting inequality relating the excess risk to the L1 norm of the difference between a function and its minimizer. The text concludes by noting that convergence in either L1 or L2 norms guarantees consistency.

children.title: Measuring the “Quality” of a Learning Algorithm
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Measuring the “Quality” of a Learning Algorithm
children.summary: This page discusses the concept of measuring the quality of a learning algorithm, arguing that consistency alone is insufficient and proposing 'Learning Rates' as a quantitative metric. It explains that algorithms can be compared by their excess risk convergence speed as sample size increases, illustrated with an expectation formula showing O(n^-alpha) decay.

children.title: Sample Complexity, Error Bounds and Tail Bounds
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Sample Complexity, Error Bounds and Tail Bounds
children.summary: This page defines three key concepts in statistical learning theory: Sample Complexity, Error Bounds, and Tail Bounds. It provides formal mathematical definitions for each, using probability notation to describe the relationship between training points (n), excess risk, and confidence levels (epsilon and delta).

children.title: Empirical Risk as a Proxy
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Empirical Risk as a Proxy
children.summary: The page discusses the concept of using empirical risk as a proxy for true expected risk when the underlying probability distribution is unknown. It defines the empirical risk function based on a sample set and demonstrates through calculation that the expectation of the empirical risk equals the true expected risk.

children.title: Empirical Vs Expected
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Empirical Risk as a Proxy/Empirical Vs Expected
children.summary: This page discusses the convergence of empirical risk to expected risk in machine learning. It mathematically demonstrates that the squared distance between the empirical mean and the expectation goes to zero as O(1/n), assuming finite variance. The text derives a formula showing that the expected squared difference between the empirical risk E_n(f) and the true risk E(f) is equal to the variance of the loss function divided by n.

children.title: Empirical Vs Expected Risk
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Empirical Risk as a Proxy/Empirical Vs Expected Risk
children.summary: The section titled 'Empirical Vs Expected Risk' discusses the relationship between empirical risk and expected risk in statistical learning theory. It presents mathematical derivations showing how the variance of the loss function relates to the difference between empirical and expected risk, particularly through inequalities involving sample size n. The content also introduces the concept of excess risk decomposition and mentions Empirical Risk Minimization as a key strategy.

children.title: Empirical Risk Minimization
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Empirical Risk Minimization
children.summary: The page presents mathematical derivations related to Empirical Risk Minimization. It defines the minimizer of empirical risk (f_n) and establishes an inequality showing that the difference between empirical risk and true risk is non-positive. The text then introduces a focus on studying generalization error, represented by the difference between expected risk and empirical risk.

children.title: Generalization Error
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/The Elements of Learning Theory/Generalization Error
children.summary: The page discusses the concept of generalization error in machine learning, specifically how to control the difference between empirical risk (E_n) and true risk (E) with respect to the number of training examples (n). It notes that this is a central topic in Statistical Learning Theory (SLT) because both terms depend on the sampled data. The text concludes by stating that a common bound involving O(1/sqrt(n)) is not generally true.

children.title: A Taxonomy of Supervised Learning Problems
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/A Taxonomy of Supervised Learning Problems
children.summary: The section titled 'A Taxonomy of Supervised Learning Problems' outlines various practical scenarios and distinctions in supervised learning. It lists four key dichotomies: parametric versus non-parametric learning, fixed design versus random design, transductive versus inductive learning, and offline/batch versus online/adversarial learning. The text concludes by noting that while these problems have different goals and assumptions, they often utilize similar tools for study and solution.

children.title: Parametric Vs Non-parametric
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/A Taxonomy of Supervised Learning Problems/Parametric Vs Non-parametric
children.summary: This page presents a comparison between parametric and non-parametric modeling approaches. It defines parametric models as those assuming a finite number of unknown parameters, with the goal of finding a parametrization that best fits observed data for purposes like identification. In contrast, it describes non-parametric models as allowing model complexity to increase with more examples, aiming for an estimator with optimal generalization performance (lowest expected risk).

children.title: Fixed Design Vs Random Design
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/A Taxonomy of Supervised Learning Problems/Fixed Design Vs Random Design
children.summary: The page presents a comparison between Fixed Design and Random Design in the context of experiment design. It defines Fixed Design as an approach where training examples are given, and the goal is to estimate conditional probabilities on prescribed inputs without assuming a distribution on the input data. A mathematical formula for the expected loss is provided. In contrast, Random Design is described as being agnostic about where the model will be tested, aiming to make good predictions with respect to the joint distribution of inputs and outputs.

children.title: Inductive Vs Transductive Learning
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/A Taxonomy of Supervised Learning Problems/Inductive Vs Transductive Learning
children.summary: This page defines and contrasts inductive versus transductive learning. It explains that transductive learning aims for good prediction performance on a specific, pre-specified set of test points provided in advance, focusing only on the risk associated with those points (represented by a mathematical formula). In contrast, inductive learning is agnostic about where the model will be tested and aims to make good predictions based on the general distribution of data.

children.title: Offline/Batch Vs Online/Adversarial Learning
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/A Taxonomy of Supervised Learning Problems/Offline∕Batch Vs Online∕Adversarial Learning
children.summary: This page defines and contrasts two learning paradigms: Offline/Batch Learning and Online/Adversarial Learning. It explains that Offline/Batch involves a finite sample of independent examples with the goal of minimizing prediction errors on new data, while Online/Adversarial involves observing inputs sequentially to propose predictions, aiming to minimize regret. A note at the bottom clarifies that the distribution can be adversarial, making the problem harder.

children.title: Wrapping up
children.path: Introduction to Statistical Learning Theory.pdf/Root/Wrapping up
children.summary: This page is a 'Wrapping up' slide from a lecture or presentation. It summarizes the topics covered in the current class, including motivations, problem formulation, learning theory, and supervised learning taxonomies. It also previews the next class topic: overfitting and regularization.
